title: Where before what
description: Why neurology looks for the lesion before it names the disease, and how that old method has to adapt when the nervous system being examined is still growing.
why: The site is named for a method, finding where the lesion is before asking what it is, and this module makes the case for that method.
objectives: Explain why clinical localization should come before imaging, and the four steps of neurologic diagnosis.
Name the eleven levels of the neuraxis and use findings to exclude levels.
Tell a destructive lesion from an irritative or releasing one by the direction of its signs.
Separate what the examination contributes (where) from what the history contributes (when).
Explain how localization sets the pretest probability that gives a scan, EEG or gene result its meaning.
Decide when several findings should be explained by one lesion and when by more than one.
Describe how development changes the meaning of findings in a child.

sections.title: Find the lesion before naming the disease
sections.content:
Long before neurology had a single effective treatment, it had a method, and that method is still the most distinctive thing it offers the rest of medicine. A cardiologist can often reason straight from a symptom to its cause. A neurologist first has to ask *where* in a long, branching system something has gone wrong. The rule is to **find the lesion before you name the disease**.

The earliest surviving record of neurologic localization is an Egyptian surgical papyrus describing a man who could not answer questions after a wound to his temple (Brazis 2011, p. 1). In the nineteenth century, Broca and Wernicke matched what patients had lost in life with what their brains showed at autopsy, an approach that became the clinicopathologic method (Brazis 2011, pp. 1-2). Hughlings Jackson added the caution that a lesion shows you where a circuit can be broken, which is a different thing from where a faculty lives.

**The four steps**

Clinical diagnosis in neurology has four steps. You recognize that a function is impaired, decide which part of the nervous system is affected, list the likely causes, and only then use tests to choose among them (Brazis 2011, p. 2). The first step raises three questions, which are whether the deficit is real, whether it is serious enough to need a workup, and whether it is neurologic at all, since a child may limp because of a sore hip (Brazis 2011, p. 3). Be generous on the first question, and unless there are clear psychiatric features, take signs at face value (Brazis 2011, p. 3).

**Why the scan comes second**

Imaging ordered without a localization finds things, and whatever it finds tends to get blamed. Congenital brain cysts are easy to see and are often blamed for symptoms they did not cause, while the real disease goes untreated (Brazis 2011, p. 1). Many disease processes sit below the resolution of any scanner, so the images have to be read alongside the clinical picture, and the two sometimes disagree (Pearl 2014, p. 1). In children, an incidental cyst or a small bright spot on MRI is common and frightening to parents. A localization made before the scan is what lets you tell them with confidence that it is not the cause.
keyPoints: Neurology's method is to find the lesion before naming the disease, asking where before asking what.
Diagnosis has four steps, which are recognizing the impaired function, localizing it, listing the likely causes and then testing among them (Brazis 2011, p. 2).
Before localizing, ask whether the deficit is real, whether it is pathological and whether it is neurologic at all (Brazis 2011, p. 3).
Localize before imaging, because unlocalized scans find incidental lesions that then get blamed for the symptoms (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Hughlings Jackson warned that a lesion shows where a circuit can be broken, which is different from where a function lives.

question.question: A 9-year-old has two months of tripping over his left foot. An outside MRI of the brain, ordered for headache, shows a small arachnoid cyst. On examination he cannot lift or evert the left foot, but inversion and hip abduction are strong, and the rest of the exam is normal. What should guide the next step?
options: The cyst, because it is the only structural abnormality found so far
The localization from the exam, which points to the left common peroneal nerve, far from the cyst
A repeat brain MRI with contrast, to see whether the cyst is growing
A spine MRI, because foot drop always comes from the spinal cord
question.explanation: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with strong inversion and hip abduction is the pattern of a common peroneal nerve lesion, so the workup belongs there, starting with nerve studies. The cyst is the kind of incidental finding that gets blamed when imaging comes first (Brazis 2011, p. 1). Spared inversion and hip abduction argue against an L5 root or cord lesion.

sections.title: The neuraxis is a list of addresses
sections.content:
Finding a lesion is like finding a house. You can locate it by its street address, or by the intersection of two streets (Brazis 2011, p. 3). Either way you need a map with named stops, and this curriculum uses eleven of them. From the top down, they are the **cerebral cortex, subcortex and deep gray matter, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, anterior horn cell, nerve root, plexus, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction and muscle**.

An intersection can pin a lesion down precisely. A third-nerve palsy on its own could sit anywhere along the nerve's course, from the brainstem to the orbit. Add a hemiparesis on the opposite side, and only one place carries both the third-nerve fibers and the corticospinal tract. That place is the cerebral peduncle of the midbrain, on the same side as the palsy (Brazis 2011, pp. 3-4).

**Use the figure above as an elimination game.** Each finding you switch on removes the levels that cannot produce it and tells you why. Weakness of the face, arm and leg removes the spinal cord at once, because the cord does not supply the face. A sensory level on the trunk removes every level except the cord. A finding earns its keep when it *excludes* a level, far more than when it merely fits one.

**How precise each level can be**

Localization is most precise low in the nervous system and least precise in the cortex (Brazis 2011, p. 4). A muscle lesion weakens that muscle, and a nerve lesion weakens its muscles and numbs its skin. A cortical lesion produces a mix of motor, sensory and behavioral findings that varies with the area involved. Low-level signs are also *consistent*, so a wasted hand muscle is there every time you look. Higher-level signs can come and go within a single examination. For language and other higher functions, the useful question is whether the patient performs a task consistently and normally each time it is tested (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

With children this matters, because a toddler's language, attention and praxis are still being built and have to be measured against age. The signs of motor unit disease already look much as they will in adulthood. The lower the level you are examining, the more you can trust a single clean sign.
keyPoints: The curriculum's eleven addresses are the cortex, subcortex, brainstem, cerebellum, cord, anterior horn, root, plexus, nerve, junction and muscle.
A lesion is often found where two damaged pathways intersect, as when a third-nerve palsy with an opposite hemiparesis places it in the midbrain (Brazis 2011, pp. 3-4).
Findings are most useful when they exclude levels, so localization works largely by elimination.
Localization is most precise low in the neuraxis and least precise in the cortex, where signs may be inconsistent (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

question.question: A 15-year-old develops, over one morning, a drooping right eyelid with the right eye turned down and out and a dilated right pupil, together with weakness of the left arm and leg. Where is the single lesion most likely to be?
options: The left internal capsule
The right oculomotor nerve in the orbit
The left side of the pons
The right cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
question.explanation: Only the right cerebral peduncle carries both the right third-nerve fibers and the still-uncrossed corticospinal fibers for the left limbs. This is the classic intersection, Weber syndrome (Brazis 2011, pp. 3-4). A left capsular lesion would spare the eye, an orbital third-nerve lesion leaves the hemiparesis unexplained, and a left pontine lesion would not touch the right third nerve.

sections.title: Negative signs, positive signs and release
sections.content:
Picture two children in the same emergency department on the same night, both with their eyes pulled hard to the left. The first, a seven-year-old girl, has a twitching left cheek and a left hand jerking in rhythm. The second, a teenager brought in from football practice, lies still with a heavy, weak right arm. Going by the eyes alone would put both problems in the same place, and one of them would be wrong.

Each frontal eye field pushes the eyes toward the opposite side, and at rest the pushes cancel. When one field is destroyed, as in a stroke, its partner pushes unopposed and the eyes drift toward the damaged side (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 43). When one field fires, as in a seizure, it drives the eyes away from itself (Pearl 2014, p. 9). After the seizure, the exhausted focus falls quiet and the eyes can swing back the other way for a while (DeMyer, p. 182). So the girl has a right frontal focus that is firing, and the teenager has a left-sided lesion that has stopped working.

Hughlings Jackson insisted that the nervous system could be understood as a sensorimotor machine, with no need to call on the soul (Pearl 2014, p. 10), and like any machine it fails in more than one way.
- **Negative signs** come from a part that has stopped, such as a weak hand, a blind half of the visual field or a patch of numb skin.
- **Positive signs** come from a part that runs too hard, like the jerking hand or the eyes driven sideways. The vagus nerve shows both, since irritating it slows the heart and destroying it lets the heart race (Pearl 2014, p. 56).
- **Release** comes from losing a part whose job was restraint (DeMyer, p. 292). An upper motor neuron lesion leaves the lower motor neuron unsupervised, so the reflexes turn brisk and the toe goes up (Pearl 2014, pp. 65, 108). The palmar grasp is normal in a newborn and fades over the first months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/introduction.html)). When it returns in an older patient with failing frontal lobes, it is a **frontal release sign** (Pearl 2014, p. 114).

:::deeper When the brain fills in a missing function
A fourth and stranger failure is a brain that does not notice an input has been lost. A patient blinded by damage to both occipital lobes may insist that they can see, and will make up answers about what is in front of them (Pearl 2014, p. 29). A patient with a right parietal lesion may say that a paralyzed left arm is moving normally, a condition Babinski named **anosognosia** (DeMyer, p. 441). The patient's own report misleads, and the way it misleads points to the lesion.
:::

The figure above sorts these possibilities by structure. Irritation often points in the opposite direction from destruction, and only some structures release or fill in.
keyPoints: A lesion can subtract function (negative signs), irritate tissue (positive signs), release what it used to restrain, or leave the brain to fill the gap.
When a frontal eye field is destroyed the eyes look toward the lesion, and when it fires in a seizure they are driven away from it (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 43).
Brisk reflexes, clonus and an upgoing toe are release signs, produced when the lower motor neuron is freed from restraint (Pearl 2014, pp. 65, 108; DeMyer, p. 292).
The newborn's palmar grasp is a normal milestone, but the same grasp returning later in frontal disease is a release sign (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam; Pearl 2014, p. 114).
Denied blindness and denied paralysis are examples of the brain filling in for a lost input (Pearl 2014, p. 29; DeMyer, p. 441).

question.question: A 7-year-old who was well at breakfast is brought in mid-event: her head and eyes are forced to the left, and her left face and arm are jerking rhythmically. Where is the lesion, and what is it doing?
options: The left frontal lobe, destroyed, so the eyes look toward the damaged side
The right pons, destroyed, so the eyes look away from it
The left frontal lobe, firing, so the eyes turn toward the focus
The right frontal lobe, firing, so the eyes are driven away from the focus
question.explanation: Rhythmic jerking is a positive sign. A right frontal seizure drives the eyes left while the right motor cortex jerks the left face and arm (Pearl 2014, pp. 9, 104). A destroyed left frontal eye field also turns the eyes left but leaves a still, weak right side. A right pontine lesion causes no jerking, and a left focus would drive the eyes right.

sections.title: Dividing the work between examination and history
sections.content:
Students tend to assume that a good history will tell them where the lesion is. For finding *where*, though, the examination matters far more, and a lesion can often be localized from the examination alone (Brazis 2011, p. 4). The examination includes the sensory findings a patient reports during it, so a complaint of numbness can be as objective as a wrist drop (Brazis 2011, p. 4).

The history contributes **time**, and the tempo suggests the kind of lesion. If a left hemiparesis arrived over minutes, think first of a vascular event or a seizure. If it evolved over a few days, think of infection or demyelination, and if it crept in over months, a tumor or a degenerative process (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Pairing *where* from the exam with *when* from the story is the backbone of this curriculum, and [[m11-where-to-what|Module 11]] builds it into a working differential.

**Three questions at the bedside**

By the end of every examination, you should be able to say where the lesion is, what the phenomenology is (the kind of disorder you are looking at), and what the likely cause is (Morris 2012, p. xxix). Commit to a diagnosis, with a short differential if you must. Listing every possible cause for fear of being wrong helps no one, and if you prove wrong you will have learned something (Morris 2012, p. xxix). Neurology relies on localization, or on recognizing the phenomenon, before it can reach a cause (Morris 2012, p. xxv). The middle question carries the disorders that have no focal lesion. A tremor, a seizure type or a tic is recognized by what it looks like.

**In a child**

Children add a second clock, so besides asking how long this has been happening, ask since when in development. A weakness present since early infancy, a skill that never arrived, and a skill that was there and has since been lost are three different stories even when today's examination looks the same, as the last section of this module shows.
keyPoints: For localization the examination matters more than the history, and sensory findings the patient reports during the exam count as examination data (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
The history supplies the tempo, with minutes suggesting a vascular event or seizure, days suggesting infection or demyelination, and months suggesting tumor or degeneration (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
End every examination by asking where the lesion is, what the phenomenology is and what the cause is, and commit to a diagnosis (Morris 2012, p. xxix).
In a child, also ask since when in development, and distinguish skills never acquired, static deficits and skills that have been lost.

question.question: A 12-year-old girl has a left hemiparesis on examination. Her parents say her left hand has become gradually clumsier over the last five months and she has started to drag her left foot. Which group of causes should head your list?
options: A tumor or a slowly progressive process
An arterial ischemic stroke
A focal seizure with post-ictal weakness
Guillain-Barré syndrome
question.explanation: The examination places the lesion in the right hemisphere or the descending motor pathway, and the history gives the tempo. Steady progression over months points first to a tumor or another slowly progressive process (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Stroke and post-ictal weakness arrive over minutes, and Guillain-Barré syndrome is peripheral and usually symmetric, so it would not cause a hemiparesis.

sections.title: Reading scans, EEGs and genes against the exam
sections.content:
Suppose two ten-year-olds have EEGs on the same afternoon, and both reports describe focal epileptiform discharges. The first has seizures that turn her eyes to the left and jerk her left face and hand, the signature of a right frontal focus, and that is where her discharges sit. The second has headaches and a normal examination, and his EEG was ordered for thoroughness. Only in the first child does the report confirm a prediction.

A test moves a belief by an amount that depends on where the belief started. The rule, named for the 18th-century English minister Thomas Bayes, is used daily in the form **pretest odds × likelihood ratio = post-test odds**. A test is best thought of as an "opinion modifier" ([Gill 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15879401/)). An identical report means different things in different children because it lands on different priors.

**The exam sets the prior**

Every localization is a prediction, and a finding at the predicted address inherits the weight of the exam, and a finding at an address the exam excluded starts near zero. Clinical diagnosis should come before ancillary tests, since only careful localization avoids the false positives of "gunshot" imaging (Brazis 2011, p. 1).

**What healthy children's tests show**

The base rates are higher than "healthy" suggests.
- Research MRI of 9- and 10-year-olds found incidental findings in 21.1% ([Li 2021](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33749724/)).
- Epileptiform discharges appeared in 6.5% of healthy 6- to 13-year-olds ([Borusiak 2010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20002145/)). Normal background patterns are often overread as epileptiform, sustaining wrong diagnoses of epilepsy ([Benbadis 2003](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12684557/)).
- Gene reports grade variants on five tiers from benign to pathogenic, with **uncertain significance** in the middle ([Richards 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25741868/)). Such a variant is not a positive result, and whether it matters depends on how well the child matches what the gene does.

**When the scan and the exam disagree**

A child weak from disease of the nerves or the neuromuscular junction has a normal brain MRI, because much disease lies outside the brain or below the resolution of imaging (Pearl 2014, p. 1). An abnormal scan explains the symptoms only if the exam put the lesion there.

**Use the figure above** by choosing a test and then a prior. The false-positive rates are sourced and the priors illustrative.

> **Rule of thumb.** After the history and examination, choose the one or two tests most likely to confirm or refute the tentative diagnosis (DeMyer, p. 539).
keyPoints: A test modifies an opinion, and in odds form the pretest odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio give the post-test odds (Gill 2005).
The localization sets the pretest probability, so a finding where the exam predicted it means far more than one at an address the exam excluded (Brazis 2011, p. 1).
Healthy children often have abnormal-looking tests, with incidental MRI findings in 21.1% at 9 to 10 years (Li 2021) and epileptiform discharges in 6.5% at 6 to 13 years (Borusiak 2010).
A variant of uncertain significance is not a positive result, and the child's phenotype decides how much weight it carries (Richards 2015).
A normal scan cannot clear disease below the resolution of imaging, and an abnormal one cannot convict without the exam (Pearl 2014, p. 1).

question.question: An 11-year-old has fainted three times in a year, each time after standing in a hot school assembly: she felt lightheaded, her vision grayed out, she slumped, and she was herself again within a minute. Her examination is normal. A routine EEG reports a few focal epileptiform discharges. What do the discharges most likely mean?
options: They prove the episodes are focal seizures, so treatment for epilepsy should start
They make syncope and epilepsy equally likely, so both should be treated
They outweigh the history, because an EEG is objective and a story is not
They are most likely a trait that some healthy children carry, and the story still points to fainting
question.explanation: Standing in the heat, then graying vision, a slump and quick recovery, is the story of a faint (Pearl 2014, p. 104), so the prior for epilepsy is low. Epileptiform discharges occur in 6.5% of healthy 6- to 13-year-olds (Borusiak 2010), so the EEG moves that prior only a little, and the tracing may have been overread (Benbadis 2003).

sections.title: One lesion or many
sections.content:
Faced with several abnormal findings, the localizer's first instinct is parsimony, which means looking for **one lesion that explains them all.** The instinct is usually right, and it drives the intersection method. A third-nerve palsy and a hemiparesis are far more likely to come from one midbrain lesion than from two unrelated ones.

Parsimony is still only a strategy, and nature doesn't promise to follow it. Hickam's dictum, usually attributed to the physician John Hickam, holds that patients can have as many diseases as they please. **Saint's triad** records the same observation, that some patients genuinely carry several unrelated conditions at once ([Hilliard 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14762188/)). The skill lies in recognizing when to stop forcing a single explanation onto findings that resist it.

**Did the findings begin together?**

Timing gives the cleanest test, since a third-nerve palsy and a hemiparesis that appear together point to the midbrain. If the palsy dates from childhood and the hemiparesis appeared decades later, the examination is probably showing two lesions that arrived at different times (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Before you merge findings into one lesion, ask whether they began together.

**Discrete lesions and system lesions**

Most localization teaching is built on **discrete lesions**, such as an infarct, a demyelinating plaque, a tumor or an abscess, each of which damages everything in one place. Other diseases attack a **functional system** instead, an array of related neurons scattered across several levels (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Parkinson disease is a system disorder that still localizes neatly to the substantia nigra, whereas a spinocerebellar degeneration has no single address. When the findings refuse to settle at one level, consider in turn several discrete lesions (as in demyelinating disease), a diffuse toxic or metabolic process, and a system degeneration. [[m10-everywhere|Module 10]] takes up the case where the answer is "everywhere".

A child with a static motor disability from early life can acquire a new and unrelated problem. The old findings have to be subtracted before the new ones can be localized, which makes the parents' account of the child's baseline part of the localization itself.
keyPoints: Start with parsimony and try to explain all the findings with one lesion.
Occam's razor has counterweights in Hickam's dictum and Saint's triad, because a patient can have more than one disease (Hilliard 2004).
Findings that began at different times may come from different lesions, so the time course decides whether to merge them (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
Discrete lesions differ from system disorders, which affect related neurons across several levels (Brazis 2011, p. 4).
In a child with a pre-existing disability, establish the baseline before localizing the new problem.

question.question: A 14-year-old with spastic diplegia since infancy (born preterm) now has three weeks of tingling and weakness creeping up from both feet, and his previously brisk ankle reflexes are now absent. What is the best way to think about the localization?
options: His long-standing diplegia explains everything, so no new localization is needed
The new findings must come from the same old brain lesion, which must be progressing
Two problems at two addresses: an old central lesion and a new peripheral one, which must be localized on its own
Reflexes are unreliable in cerebral palsy, so the change can be ignored
question.explanation: His static central lesion produces brisk reflexes. New ascending sensory and motor symptoms with loss of those reflexes are a change in kind, pointing to a new peripheral process such as a polyneuropathy. The findings began at different times (Brazis 2011, p. 4). A static brain lesion does not abolish reflexes, and dismissing the change is how a second diagnosis gets missed.

sections.title: Localization in a developing child
sections.content:
An adult's nervous system holds still while you examine it, but a child's keeps changing. That makes **development the fourth dimension of pediatric localization**. The same finding can be normal at one age and a sign of disease at another, and a fixed lesion can produce signs that change as the brain around it grows.

**When age changes the meaning**

The upgoing big toe is a cornerstone sign of corticospinal tract damage, yet it can be normal in the first year of life, while the corticospinal tracts are still being myelinated ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)). The closer an infant is to one year, the more consistently the toe goes down (DeMyer, p. 282). Handedness runs the other way, since a hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/06month.html)). The baby who reaches only with the right hand may be telling you about the left.

**Fixed lesions with changing signs**

Cerebral palsy is defined as a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture attributed to **non-progressive** disturbances in the developing fetal or infant brain ([Rosenbaum 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17370477/)). The clinical picture changes as the child grows, and infants with cerebral palsy may look hypotonic before spasticity appears (DeMyer, p. 273). A floppy infant who becomes a stiff toddler need not have a progressive disease. The maturing motor system has revealed a lesion that was there all along.

**Localization in time**

In children you localize along a time axis as well as a spatial one, and part of the work is deciding which of three stories the child is in.

- **Static** problems are present from early life and not worsening, though their expression may change with growth.
- **Progressive** problems are getting worse, which demands a search for an active process.
- **Regressive** problems involve the loss of skills once acquired. This is the most urgent pattern of all, because it implies the nervous system is being damaged now.

No single examination can tell these three apart. The history, the developmental record and repeated examinations can, which is why in child neurology the second visit is often more informative than the first.
keyPoints: Development is the fourth dimension of pediatric localization, because the meaning of a finding depends on the child's age.
An upgoing toe is normal in the first year while the corticospinal tracts myelinate (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).
Cerebral palsy comes from a non-progressive lesion, yet its signs evolve, and hypotonia may come before spasticity (Rosenbaum 2007; DeMyer, p. 273).
Classify the time course as static, progressive or regressive, and treat regression as the most urgent.

question.question: At a 9-month check, a mother says her baby always reaches with the right hand and seems to ignore toys offered on the left. The baby is otherwise well and sitting. What is the right interpretation and next step?
options: Early right-handedness, a normal variant; reassure
A possible left hemiparesis; examine carefully for asymmetry of tone, reflexes and the parachute response, and arrange brain imaging if confirmed
A visual problem in the left eye; refer to ophthalmology only
A sign of autism; refer for developmental assessment
question.explanation: Hand preference before 12 months is abnormal and points to weakness of the other hand (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam), so examine for a left hemiparesis, which in an infant often follows a perinatal stroke in the right hemisphere. Calling it early handedness is false reassurance. Vision is worth checking, but referring only to ophthalmology skips the likelier motor cause, and nothing here suggests autism.

quiz.question: A medical student, keen to be efficient, orders a brain MRI on every child with a new neurologic complaint before examining them. Which step of clinical diagnosis has been skipped, and what is the main risk?
options: Recognition of impaired function; the risk is missing the diagnosis entirely
Listing likely causes; the risk is ordering too few tests
Localization; the risk is that incidental findings get blamed for the symptoms while the real lesion is missed
Ancillary testing; the risk is radiation exposure
quiz.explanation: Localization is the second of four steps, after recognizing the impaired function and before listing causes or ordering tests (Brazis 2011, p. 2). Imaging without it produces false positives, such as congenital cysts blamed for unrelated symptoms (Brazis 2011, p. 1). Recognition has already happened, since the child came with a complaint, and MRI involves no ionizing radiation.

quiz.question: On a busy ward round, a resident examines a 7-year-old with a headache and documents only 'neuro exam WNL'. What is the problem with this note?
options: Nothing, if the child is well
It should say 'non-focal' instead
It records a conclusion instead of what was actually tested and found, so no one can tell what was examined
It should include a numerical score such as the Glasgow Coma Scale
quiz.explanation: A recorded examination should show the next reader what was tested and what was found, and 'within normal limits' hides both. 'WNL' is not an acceptable record of the examination (DeMyer, p. 604), and findings should be recorded objectively before they are interpreted (DeMyer, p. 36). 'Non-focal' has the same flaw, and a coma score has no place in a well, alert child.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old with a new speech problem repeats some phrases perfectly and fails on others of similar difficulty. What should the examiner conclude about repetition?
options: Repetition is normal, because he can do it
Repetition is impaired, because higher functions should be judged by whether they are consistently normal
The test is invalid in children and should not be recorded
He is not trying, so the finding is functional
quiz.explanation: Higher-level signs can be inconsistent within one examination, so the question is whether the patient performs a task consistently and normally (Brazis 2011, p. 4). Recording repetition as normal because some phrases succeed misses the deficit. Repetition can be tested at 10, and inconsistency at higher levels is expected in organic disease, so it does not by itself suggest a functional disorder.

quiz.question: An 8-month-old born at term has an upgoing big toe on both sides when the sole is stroked. The rest of the examination, development and tone are normal. What does the plantar response mean?
options: It is consistent with normal development at this age
It localizes to the spinal cord and needs urgent imaging
It localizes to both cerebral hemispheres
It shows a peripheral nerve problem
quiz.explanation: An upgoing toe is normal in the first year while the corticospinal tracts myelinate (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam), and the flexor response becomes more constant as the infant nears one year (DeMyer, p. 282). In a developmentally normal 8-month-old with symmetric findings, it does not localize, though reproducible asymmetry would. A peripheral nerve lesion cannot produce an extensor plantar response at any age.

quiz.question: Two children have identical MRI reports describing a small area of abnormal signal in the left frontal lobe. The first has had focal seizures with jerking of the right arm and now a weak right hand. The second was scanned for headaches and has a normal examination. How should the same finding be weighed in each?
options: It is far more likely to be the cause in the first child, because the exam predicted a lesion at that address
It means the same in both, because the reports are identical
It is more likely to matter in the second child, because a normal exam cannot rule a lesion out
Neither can be interpreted until a repeat scan shows whether it changes
quiz.explanation: The reports are identical but the priors are not. In the first child the exam localized to the left motor cortex before the scan, so the finding lands on a high pretest probability (Gill 2005). In the second child nothing predicted a lesion, and 21.1% of research MRIs in 9- to 10-year-olds show incidental findings (Li 2021). A repeat scan does not replace that reasoning.

opener.parable: Imagine posting a letter with the right name on the envelope but no street or town. It isn't exactly lost, but nobody can deliver it until someone works out where it should go. A child's symptoms often arrive in clinic in the same state, and many of the tests we reach for are really attempts to guess the address.
opener.history: The oldest localization on record comes from Egypt, where a surgeon writing more than four thousand years ago described a man with a wound in the temple who could not answer when spoken to. Much later, the Hippocratic physicians recorded that an injury to the left side of the brain weakens the right side of the body.
